USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: The US should hold its current tariff posture without further escalation for now, but maintain the threat of additional tariffs as leverage. The midterm elections are weeks away and the current strategy is politically popular; there is no reason to back down, but also no reason to trigger a further spiral before seeing whether China is willing to come to the table after November.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of +0.35 reflects a moderate but not existential threat to US interests. The trade war has already escalated to cover $250 billion in Chinese imports (roughly half of US-China trade), with China retaliating on $110 billion of the $130 billion in US goods it imports (Fox Business/Motley Fool analysis). Key US sectors are feeling pain: soybean prices are down 20% (Brookings), farmers in the Midwest are hit hard, and Boeing and auto exporters face significant Chinese retaliation. However, as Brookings' David Dollar notes, the overall macro impact is 'a minor blip' for the US economy, and the Trump administration views the trade war as a winning midterm strategy. The US has structural leverage — it imports far more from China ($506B) than it exports ($130B), meaning China cannot fully match US tariff escalation. At the same time, the situation is not yet dangerous enough to warrant concession: no high-level negotiations are scheduled, China has signaled it will not 'cave,' and the administration has threatened to tariff the remaining $267 billion if China retaliates further. The action score of -1 (hold at current escalation level) reflects the judgment that the US should maintain maximum pressure but pause further escalation — the $200B round (Sept 24) is still ramping from 10% to 25% at year-end, giving built-in leverage. Pushing to tariff 100% of trade now would risk broader consumer backlash and ally defection without clear negotiating payoff.
key_factors: $250B in tariffs already imposed on Chinese goods, covering ~50% of bilateral trade
China has retaliated on $110B of $130B in US imports, nearly exhausting its retaliatory capacity
Soybean prices down 20%, Midwest farmers and auto exporters feeling real pain
Overall macro impact described as 'minor blip' for US economy (Brookings)
No high-level negotiations scheduled; China unlikely to make major concessions
Trump admin views trade war as politically advantageous ahead of 2018 midterms
Sept 24 tariffs on $200B set to rise from 10% to 25% at year-end, providing built-in escalation leverage
US has threatened additional $267B if China retaliates further

sources_cited.excerpt: Effective Sept. 24, President Trump announced a 10% tariff on $200 billion in Chinese imports. That tariff is currently 10%, but at the end of 2018, that's expected to rise to 25%.

The price of soybeans is already down 20 percent. This is not a big hit for the overall U.S. economy but it will hurt some specific sectors. On the whole this is a minor blip so the Trump administration will probably not change its strategy soon.
This second round of Chinese tariffs is going to now cover $110 billion of the $130 billion of U.S.-China trade -- again, almost 100% of the entire trading relationship.
The U.S. buys $506 billion worth of goods from China but only exports $130 billion, leaving a trade deficit of $375 billion between the two countries.
